t: The landings were the largest seaborne invasion in history: a fleet of 6,939 vessels from eight navies, nearly 160,000 troops across the Channel on D-Day and 875,000 landed by the end of June.
Allied casualties on the first day were at least 10,000, with 4,414 confirmed dead; German casualties are estimated at 4,000 to 9,000. Omaha, with its high cliffs, had the most Allied casualties.

Many of the first-day objectives were not met: Caen, a major objective, was not completely captured until 21 July, and the Germans never achieved Hitler's stated aim of throwing the Allies back into the sea.
dyk: The day was chosen because the tides, the hour and the moon allowed only a few dates a month; when storms forced a postponement from 5 June, the next suitable dates were two weeks later, and a major storm struck the Normandy coast from 19 to 22 June.
ev: The decision to undertake a cross-channel invasion within the next year is taken at the Trident Conference in Washington in May
Eisenhower and Montgomery first see the plan and insist on widening the landings to five divisions
On 4 June Eisenhower meets Group Captain James Stagg, whose forecast of improving weather leads him to go ahead on 6 June
On 6 June airborne troops land after midnight and the amphibious landings on the five beaches begin about 06:30
On 12 June the five beachheads are connected
German forces retreat east across the Seine, closing Operation Overlord

f.date: 6 June 1944 (D-Day), after a postponement of 24 hours from the 5 June first chosen
f.place: An 80-kilometre stretch of the Normandy coast of France, divided into the sectors Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, with airborne landings inland
f.sides: The Allies under General Dwight D. Eisenhower, with General Bernard Montgomery commanding the land forces, nearly 160,000 troops crossing the Channel on the day; Germany under Hitler, with Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt as Supreme Commander West and Field Marshal Erwin Rommel commanding Army Group B
f.outcome: The Allies established a beachhead at each of the five sites on the first day, but Carentan, Saint-Lô, Bayeux and Caen stayed in German hands; the five beachheads were not connected until 12 June.
